title: Automatic radiometric normalization of multitemporal satellite imagery with the iteratively re-weighted MAD transformation
relevance: IR-MAD automatically finds no-change pixels shared by two images and fits a per-band linear transform from them, and it is explicitly INVARIANT TO GAIN AND OFFSET DIFFERENCES IN THE MEASURING DEVICE - which is exactly the defect we just measured, where GRVI over identical ground reads 0.1146 in 2019 King County and 0.8919 in 2019 NAIP. It is the standard remedy for the problem and it requires no reference targets and no field data, only the image pairs we already hold. IMPORTANT LIMIT: it corrects AFFINE differences, so if our cast comes from gamma, JPEG compression or per-frame colour balancing it will only partly work - which makes testing it a diagnostic of what kind of distortion we have.

title: Relaxation-Based Radiometric Normalization for Multitemporal Cross-Sensor Satellite Images
relevance: Targets the CROSS-SENSOR case specifically, which is ours rather than the easier same-sensor multitemporal case that most normalization work assumes, and our 17 acquisitions come from at least four distinct providers with EagleView and changing King County contractors behind them. It matters because the strict no-change assumption underlying IR-MAD is weakest exactly where our series is longest, over 24 years during which real canopy change is large. Gives a relaxed alternative to test against IR-MAD rather than a single method to adopt blind.

title: Radiometric Normalization Using a Pseudo-Invariant Polygon Features-Based Algorithm with Contemporaneous Imagery
relevance: Uses pseudo-invariant POLYGONS rather than pixels, which suits us because we already hold building footprints and an impervious raster - roofs and pavement are the classic invariant targets and we can supply them directly instead of estimating them. It offers a route that does not assume the scene is mostly unchanged, and our scene demonstrably is not over 24 years. It also gives a cheap validity check on any normalization we apply: canopy over impervious is our worst-performing class, so a normalization fitted on impervious polygons must be shown NOT to have simply moved that error around.
